answer.label: Not Thomas Edison — condensed from Sir Joshua Reynolds
answer.authorDates: 1723–1792 · English portrait painter & first President of the Royal Academy
answer.sourceLine: The thought traces to Reynolds’s Twelfth Discourse (delivered 1784, published 1797), whose phrase “evade and shuffle off real labour, —the real labour of thinking” was later condensed by critic Irving Babbitt (1910) into an aphorism. Edison hung the line in his labs but credited it to Reynolds; the popular one-line wording is a paraphrase, not Edison’s own words. Per Quote Investigator.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Placards in his labs, reported Jan. 1921 — credited to Reynolds

source.excerpt: “A provision of endless apparatus, a bustle of infinite enquiry and research, or even the mere mechanical labour of copying, may be employed, to evade and shuffle off real labour, —the real labour of thinking.”
trail: Quote Investigator traces the aphorism to Reynolds’s 1784/1797 Twelfth Discourse, condensed by critic Irving Babbitt in 1910.
B. C. Forbes reported in The American Magazine (January 1921) that Edison posted the line in his laboratories — attributing it to “Sir Joshua Reynolds,” per QI.
Wikiquote lists the exact popular wording under “Misattributed,” noting Edison liked and posted it but did not originate it.
source.excerptNote: Reynolds’s original 1797 sentence — the seed of the modern aphorism. The compact “no expedient … to avoid the labor of thinking” form is a much later condensation.
source.rightsNote: Reynolds’s underlying 1797 Discourse XII is long in the public domain, but the compact popular wording (“no expedient … to avoid the labor of thinking”) is an evolved paraphrase not tied to a single identifiable pre-1931 work in this exact form, so no clean copyright status can be asserted for the line as quoted.

author.name: Sir Joshua Reynolds
author.heading: Sir Joshua Reynolds
author.metaLine: 1723–1792 · English portrait painter & first President of the Royal Academy
author.bio: Sir Joshua Reynolds was the leading English portraitist of the 18th century and the founding President of the Royal Academy of Arts. His annual Discourses to Academy students — delivered 1769–1790 — are landmarks of art theory, and it is a sentence from his Twelfth Discourse, on avoiding “the real labour of thinking,” that later generations compressed into the aphorism now pinned on Edison.

misattribution.heading: How Edison got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook misattribution: Edison admired the line, hung it around his laboratories, and openly credited Sir Joshua Reynolds — but later writers dropped Reynolds’s name and left Edison holding the quote.

items.why: Wikiquote files this exact sentence under “Misattributed,” noting Edison liked and posted it but did not write it. Dale Carnegie’s How to Stop Worrying and Start Living (1948) helped cement the Edison credit, per QI.

The idea comes from Reynolds’s Twelfth Discourse (1784/1797): “to evade and shuffle off real labour, —the real labour of thinking.” Critic Irving Babbitt condensed it toward the modern aphorism in 1910, per Quote Investigator.

misattribution.truthLine: Edison posted it and credited Reynolds; the compact one-liner is a paraphrase of Reynolds by way of Babbitt, not Edison’s own sentence. See Quote Investigator.

context.heading: Why the line stuck to Edison
lead: Edison was America’s emblem of hard, practical work, so an aphorism praising mental effort felt like something he should have said. He did display it — but as a quotation from Reynolds, not as his own coinage.

The sentence itself is a slow accretion: Reynolds’s dense 1797 clause about “the real labour of thinking” was streamlined by Irving Babbitt in 1910, then circulated as placards and mottos until the words hardened into the crisp modern one-liner — and the original author’s name fell away.
detailsBody: Reynolds (1797): “…to evade and shuffle off real labour, —the real labour of thinking.”
Babbitt (1910): “there is scarcely any expedient to which man will not resort in order to ‘evade and shuffle off real labor.’”
Forbes/Edison (1921): “There is no expedient to which a man will not resort to avoid the real labor of thinking.”
Modern popular form: drops “real” and swaps “resort” for “go” — “…will not go to avoid the labor of thinking.”
context.pull: Edison hung the words on his wall and signed them “Reynolds.” History erased the credit anyway.
